cards.text: The LORD is still giving Moses the plans for the tabernacle, and the tent, the altar and the courtyard are all mapped out. Now He turns to people. He wants Moses' brother Aaron brought to him from among the Israelites, along with Aaron's sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.

cards.question: Aaron and his four sons are brought to Moses to serve God as ___.

cards.text: Now, Aaron can't show up to serve in just anything. God tells Moses to make holy garments for his brother.

cards.question: God tells Moses to make holy garments for Aaron. What are they meant to give him?
Moses isn't sewing these himself. Who does God tell him to instruct to make Aaron's garments?

cards.text: And God says He's the One who filled those craftsmen with a spirit of wisdom. Their skill came from God, friend, and mine came from burning a WHOLE batch in this bakery and pretending it was on purpose.
God lists the garments: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban and a sash. SIX pieces, and I own an apron and a hat and still can't decide what to wear in the morning.

cards.question: God says these holy garments are just for Aaron and nobody else.

cards.text: They'll use gold, fine linen and blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and the ephod comes first, with two shoulder pieces and a woven waistband made all in one piece. GOLD thread, friend, and my fanciest look ever was a 25-cent price sticker.
Then God tells Moses to take two onyx stones and engrave names on them.

cards.question: Whose names get engraved on the two onyx stones?
Twelve names on two onyx stones means six names on one stone and ___ on the other.

cards.text: The names go on in the order the sons were born, engraved the way a gem cutter engraves a seal, then set in gold filigree. Engraved like a seal means they won't blur, and as a stamper who used to stamp blurry, I'm a LITTLE jealous.

cards.question: The two onyx stones go on the front of Aaron's turban.
Aaron carries the names of the sons of Israel on his two shoulders as a ___ before the LORD.

cards.text: Then come gold filigree settings and two chains of pure gold, braided like cord and attached to the settings. Aaron's carrying twelve tribes on his shoulders, and I used to complain about a stack of junk-drawer takeout menus on my back.
Next up, the breastpiece of judgment. Sounds serious, friend, and it is.

cards.question: The breastpiece is made with the same workmanship as the ephod, with gold, colored yarn and fine linen.
When the breastpiece is folded over double, what shape does it have to be?

cards.text: It's a span long and a span wide, with four rows of gemstones set in gold, from a ruby, a topaz and an emerald on top down to a beryl, an onyx and a jasper. TWELVE stones, and the shiniest thing in my old junk drawer was a dead battery.

cards.question: There are twelve stones on the breastpiece. What's engraved on each one?

answers.text: The name of one of the twelve tribes
A word from the Law of Moses
The name of one of the elders

cards.text: Then come braided chains of pure gold, gold rings at the corners, and a cord of blue yarn tying the breastpiece to the ephod so it doesn't swing out. God thought of EVERYTHING, friend, even the wobble.
Now here's the part I love. Whenever Aaron enters the Holy Place, he carries the names of the sons of Israel on that breastpiece.

cards.question: When Aaron enters the Holy Place wearing the breastpiece, where are the names of the sons of Israel?
The names on the breastpiece are a reminder before the LORD only on Aaron's first day as priest.

cards.text: And God tells Moses to put the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece too. Try saying that three times fast, friend, because I did, and my mustache tied itself in a knot.

cards.question: The Urim and Thummim go in the breastpiece. Where does that put them whenever Aaron comes before the LORD?
Aaron will continually carry the ___ of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD.

cards.text: Next is the robe of the ephod, made entirely of blue cloth. It's got a woven collar around the opening at the top so it won't tear, which is more planning than anybody ever put into my apron.

cards.question: Pomegranates made of yarn go all the way around the robe's lower hem. What goes between them?

cards.text: Gold bells and pomegranates take turns all the way around the hem, and Aaron has to wear this robe whenever he ministers. Mags would LOVE this robe, friend, because nobody's sneaking anywhere in it.

cards.question: The robe's sound will be heard when Aaron ___ or ___ the sanctuary before the LORD.
God gives these instructions about the robe and its sound so that Aaron will not die.

cards.text: Then God tells Moses to make a plate of pure gold and engrave words on it like a seal.

cards.question: What gets engraved on the gold plate?
The gold plate is fastened with a blue cord to the front of Aaron's turban.

cards.text: That plate sits on Aaron's forehead, and it's always there. God says it's so Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things the Israelites consecrate in all their holy gifts.

cards.question: Aaron bears the iniquity of the Israelites' holy gifts with that gold plate on his forehead. What does God say it's for?

answers.text: So they may be acceptable before the LORD
So Aaron may rule over all the tribes
So the people may never sin again

cards.text: Aaron gets a fine linen tunic, a fine linen turban and an embroidered sash, and his sons get tunics, sashes and headbands. Even the HEADBANDS made it into the plans, friend, so I'm feeling real good about this chef's hat.

cards.question: God says the garments for Aaron's sons are also to give them glory and splendor.
Once Moses puts these garments on Aaron and his sons, what does God tell him to do next?

cards.text: Last come linen undergarments, from waist to thigh. Aaron and his sons wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar, so that they will not incur guilt and die.

cards.question: God says the rule about the linen undergarments is to be a ___ statute for Aaron and his descendants.

cards.text: That's every last stitch of Aaron's outfit. But hold on to your apron, friend, because God's not done talking to Moses yet.

findings.problem: The opening card states facts from outside the passage: the tent, the altar and the courtyard are already mapped out (Exodus 26-27). They carry no reference. The card cites only Exodus 28:1.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: "Aaron can't show up to serve in just anything" adds a reason for the garments that the text doesn't give. The text's stated purpose is "to give him glory and splendor" (28:2) and his consecration (28:3).

rule.text: Reasons: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The question gives its own answer. It says there are twelve names and six go on one stone, so simple arithmetic rules out "four" and "eight." The card tests subtraction instead of the passage.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The card cites Exodus 28:13-14, but its line about Aaron carrying names on his shoulders comes from 28:12, so the citation is too narrow. The line also says Aaron carries "twelve tribes." Verse 12 says he bears the names of the sons of Israel.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: The right answer, "The name of one of the twelve tribes," repeats "twelve" from the question ("There are twelve stones"). Neither wrong answer does, so the right one stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: Exodus 28 is almost entirely garment specifications, which resemble "building plans" in the long-stretch list. Some parts are already summed up (the gemstones in 28:17-20 and the rings and chains in 28:22-28). Others get choice cards on construction details: the breastpiece workmanship (stop 2 card 2), its square shape (stop 2 card 3), six names per stone (stop 1 card 12), gold bells between the pomegranates (stop 3 card 2) and the blue cord on the turban (stop 3 card 8). The docs don't say what to do when a whole assigned passage is mostly long-stretch detail. They say a stretch is summed up in one card, never gets a stop of its own, and never gets a choice card.
findings.question: When an entire passage is mostly detail like building or garment plans, how much of it counts as a long stretch? Can choice cards ask about construction details like shapes, materials and fastenings, or only about stated purposes like the memorial, over his heart, so that he will not die, and HOLY TO THE LORD?
